name: Name, Role, Value
explanation: Every interface component needs three things exposed to assistive technology: a name, a role, and its current state or value. The name says what the control is, like "Submit" or "Email address." The role says what kind of control it is, like a button or a checkbox. The state or value says its current condition, like checked, expanded, or a typed-in value. When any of these changes, that update must also be exposed, so assistive technology knows about it right away. Standard HTML elements like `<button>` and `<input>` provide all of this automatically. Custom-built widgets, made from generic `<div>` or `<span>` elements, don't, and need ARIA attributes added by hand.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users depend entirely on this exposed information to understand a page. Without a role, a screen reader can't tell a user that something is a button versus a plain block of text. Without a name, a control gets announced as just "button," with no clue what it does. Without exposed state changes, a screen reader user has no way to know a checkbox got checked, or a menu opened, unless they happen to notice a visual change they can't actually see. This is one of the most common accessibility failures, since it's easy to build a custom widget that looks and works fine visually while exposing none of this to assistive technology.

codeExample.bad: Subscribe to newsletter

howToTest: Turn on a screen reader and tab to each interactive control on the page. For each one, listen for three things: what it's called, what kind of control it is, and its current state. If a control announces only "button" with no name, or gives no indication of a checked, expanded, or selected state, this fails. A browser's accessibility inspector panel is a faster way to check the same thing. It shows the computed name, role, and state for any element, without needing a full screen reader session.

check.question: A custom dropdown menu is built entirely from styled `<div>` elements. It has no `role`, `aria-expanded`, or accessible name set anywhere, but it works fine with a mouse. Does this pass SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value?
choices: Yes, because it works correctly for mouse users
No, because assistive technology has no way to determine its role, name, or open/closed state
Yes, because div elements are valid HTML
It depends only on whether the dropdown has a visible label nearby
